notes.title: Chapter map: Prompt ops

headings.text: 🌳 Where should this prompt live, and how does it ship?

notes.html:
How a prompt that passed its tests reaches users, and how you get it back. Note 83 decides where the text lives; 84 gives each edit an address; 86 releases it in stages; 88 keeps that one artifact when tenants and locales multiply; 87 is the forced release, a new model; 89 watches what shipped; 85 and 90 name the tools and who may press the button. Read each arrow as a sentence: a version is released by a label move.

Green = CORE, blue = SUPPORTING, yellow = BREADTH, grey = another section.

Reading order:83 code vs config84 prompt versioning86 decoupled release88 multi-tenant and localised87 model-upgrade migration89 observability85 registries and tooling90 governance

Owners

Ideas several notes touch, and the one note that explains each. Rows pointing out of the section close an overlap.

Idea Owner note
Where the string is resolved; who holds the pen; the hybrid: repo as source, CI as only publisher, people move labels 83 code vs config
An immutable version and a movable label; the resolved version in every trace; same name, same contract 84 prompt versioning
The release states; sticky assignment; rollback time is propagation, not the API call; canary vs A/B 86 decoupled release
Request valid first, then prompt held fixed; triage by what an output reaches 87 model-upgrade migration
Fork the variables, not the prompt; template and config as two lifecycles; tenant text after the static prefix 88 multi-tenant and localised
Two streams, one join key; free signals before a judge; cost per success, by version 89 observability
Which product does what, and who owns it now 85 registries, with this map's Landscape
Authoring vs promoting; protected labels; code owners 90 governance
The unit that ships is a tuple, not a string the prompt as a coupled system, not these notes
Which change runs which suite; contracts vs measurements regression suites and CI, not these notes
A/B test design and sample size A/B testing and error bars and paired tests (LLM-Production), not these notes
Versioning and canaries across the platform bundle versioning and rollout (LLM-Production), not these notes
Tracing, dashboards, pipelines, sampling infrastructure LLM observability (LLM-Production) and agent tracing (Agentic), not these notes
Quotas and rate limits per tenant API-level multi-tenancy (LLM-Production), not these notes
Slot syntax and template hazards prompt templating, not these notes
Instruction language vs content language cross-lingual prompting, not these notes
Per-family model differences model-family differences, not these notes
The cost-per-call sum cost modelling, not these notes
Reproducing a decision for a regulator compliance and auditability, not these notes
Build or buy the tooling build vs buy, not these notes
Why tenant text in a slot is untrusted prompt injection, not these notes

Changed on 31 Oct 2026:

  • No tier changed. Note 84 stays CORE, 85 and 90 stay BREADTH, the rest SUPPORTING. Nothing merged, so the pillar's counts are unchanged by this section.
  • Note 89 sits at watch, as the index proposed; the other seven are at ship.
  • The system-design block left note 84. It had two architecture diagrams and a capacity table; one Design answer remains, linking the reference architecture.
  • Rollback is no longer "equal to the cache TTL". Under stale-while-revalidate a quiet process serves the old version on its next request, however late; note 86 shows it running.
  • A commit SHA can be the join key. The older note said it couldn't reach a trace; it can, if you stamp it. Note 84 now says so, and prefers a content hash.
  • Unsourced numbers were dropped: "10–40 minute" deploys, "tens of ms" fetches, "10–20% of prompts need attention", and a 0.4% to 11% parse-failure trace.

Older text of every note is in 08-Prompt-engineering/_superseded/09-Prompt Ops/.

Where should this prompt live, and how does it ship?

Every leaf sits behind the same regression gate. The tree picks a channel, not a level of testing.

  • Files in Git (83): if non-engineers need to edit, or a deploy is slower than your rollback target, climb.
  • Stays with the parser (84): if the parser accepts both shapes, a labelled rollout of the new shape becomes safe.
  • 🚩 Flag platform (86): if you need prompt diffs and per-version evals that it doesn't offer, a registry fits better.
  • 🔖 Hybrid (85): if you can't accept the runtime dependency, ship prompts in the image and use the registry for authoring only.

At a glance

Practice What it adds Cost Needs Fails as Enforced by
Prompts in code a build as the test boundary a deploy per change engineers as editors fixes queue behind the release train CI on the build
Hybrid registry a second release channel a runtime dependency CI as the only publisher a pointer moved to something untested the write token, the gate
Versions and labels an address for each edit one field per trace one client library a blended rate behind one label an append-only store
Staged release a way back with no build two versions during a move sticky assignment rollback slower than promised the rollout controller
Tenant slots one artifact, N rows tiered eval coverage a schema an unvalidated slot, a cold cache validation before render
Model migration a measured per-prompt decision an eval run per prompt a golden set, a pinned model both factors changed at once the gate, the provider's date
Two-stream logging metrics with no customer text a sampled text store the version id on every record an archive that joins to nothing the client library, redaction
Promotion rights a named person on every move a slower promotion roles, an audit trail an advisory gate protected labels, code owners

Lineage

Year What appeared What it fixed Status

Mar 2023 Dated model snapshots (gpt-4-0314) a model that moved under you 🟢 Established
Jan 2024 Hosted prompt versions (Langfuse), then deployment labels prompts that needed a deploy to change 🟢 Established
Jan 2025 OpenTelemetry describes GenAI conventions, in development every tool naming its fields differently 🟡 Maturing
Jun 2025 OpenAI reusable prompts in the Responses API a provider-hosted version store ⚪ Fading: shutdown 30 Nov 2026
2025–26 Consolidation: Humanloop shut down, Langfuse and Promptfoo acquired — 🟡 Maturing
Jun 2026 OpenAI deprecates prompt objects for prompts in code prompts outside the release process 🟡 Maturing
Oct 2026 Anthropic API version 2026-10-21 rejects sampling parameters on every model settings that no longer steered the model 🔵 Emerging

Landscape (as of Oct 2026)

Read from each page on 31 Oct 2026. Dates move; re-check before quoting. Partner platforms set their own schedules.

Model retirement and what a migration breaks.

Anthropic OpenAI Google (Gemini API)
Notice at least 60 days for publicly released models; dates cover Anthropic-operated platforms, while Bedrock and Google-managed Vertex set their own at least 6 months for generally available models; 3 for specialised variants; previews "such as 2 weeks" listed dates are the earliest possible; exact date given later; previews at least 2 weeks

Sampling parameters temperature, top_p, top_k return 400 in API version 2026-10-21, on every model; earlier versions reject non-default values on Claude 4.7 and later remove them when reasoning effort isn't none (GPT-6 family guide) ignored with a deprecation warning on Gemini 4 and 3.6+; guide says to remove them

Source deprecations · Opus 5.5 migration · API version guide · models deprecations · latest model deprecations · models · prompting

Tools.

Tool What it is Versions and release Governance and caching Ownership, status
Langfuse open-source tracing plus prompt management immutable numbered versions; labels; production is the default, latest tracks the newest protected labels: Enterprise, or Pro with the Teams add-on; audit logs: Enterprise; SDK cache: 60 s default, stale-while-revalidate acquired by ClickHouse, 16 Jan 2026; no planned licence change

Braintrust evaluation platform each save is a version; environments map a version to dev, staging, production code can pin a version or load an environment docs moved to docs.braintrust.dev
LaunchDarkly AgentControl feature flags for prompts and model settings variations; targeting rules, percentage and guarded rollouts an add-on; not in federal environments formerly AI Configs; API unchanged, older names persist in code

Standard: OpenTelemetry GenAI conventions moved out of the main repository to their own; gen_ai.* attributes are marked Development, including gen_ai.prompt.name and gen_ai.prompt.version, which are conditionally required when a named prompt is used.

Not read in this pass: LangSmith's prompt hub, Vertex AI and Bedrock prompt management. No note here depends on them.

Four bullets

  • The one big idea: a prompt release is a pointer move guarded by a gate. The text is immutable, the pointer is the only thing that moves, and the id travels with every request. Then "what changed?" has an answer and "put it back" takes one action. Everything else in this section either feeds that loop or watches it.
  • The two most-confused pairs: a version vs a label (84: never changes, against moves by design) · a canary vs an A/B test (86: is it safe to continue, against did users behave differently).
  • Ten minutes before an interview: note 84's pipeline and the Break it with the blended rate, note 86's release states and the quiet pod, note 87's triage flowchart, note 89's two streams, and this map's tree.
  • Cross-section links: the gate is regression suites and CI; the tuple is the prompt as a coupled system; the architecture is the prompt-layer reference architecture. Content gaps: no note on rolling out a change to a prompt's output contract (a parser that reads both shapes is a rule row in notes 84 and 86), and none on detecting that a provider changed behaviour behind a pinned id (nightly runs in note 78 touch it).

notes.title: Prompts as Code vs Prompts as Config — Who Holds the Pen, and What CI Actually Tested
notes.html:
References

OpenAI: prompting · OpenAI: migrate from prompt objects · Langfuse: prompt management · Chip Huyen: building a generative AI platform

TL;DR

In the repo, a prompt ships with its build, so you serve exactly what CI tested, and every change waits for a deploy. In a registry, it changes without a deploy and non-engineers can edit it, and what you serve may not be what you tested. So the question is who holds the pen and how fast a change must land. The usual answer is both: author in the repo, publish from CI, release by label.

Stage:decidewriteassemblecallshapeevaluateshipwatchdesign time
Flow:who edits? how fast must a change land? ─engineers, deploys are quick enoughprompt in code
─others edit, or deploys are too slowrepo stays the sourceCI publishes tested versionspeople move labels only

Recall

Prompt Answer
The deciding axis? Who edits, and must prompt release be independent of code release?
What does code-first guarantee? You serve what CI tested, in lockstep with its parser.
The hybrid? Repo is the source; CI is the only publisher; humans only move labels.

The idea

CI validated version 12. At 4 pm someone moved a pointer in the registry UI, and production now renders version 17 against a parser that never saw it. Nothing failed to build, because nothing was built.

That's the cost of config. Code has its own: a domain expert spots a wrong policy line, and the fix waits behind a pull request, a CI run and a release train, so the wrong line stays live for days.

The two positions differ in where the string is resolved. In code, it's fixed at build time, so the build is the test boundary. In a registry, it's fixed at request time, so nothing downstream knows what was tested.

The trade: a registry buys a second release channel and pays for it with a runtime dependency and a gap between what was tested and what runs; the gate has to close that gap, or you've only made bad changes faster.

How it works

The hybrid keeps both properties by limiting who can do what on each side.

An untested prompt never becomes a version, so the fastest thing a panicking engineer can do is point a label at something tested.

Rule What actually happens
Output contracts stay in code A prompt whose output a parser reads must ship with that parser. A registry can't make the two moves atomic.
A UI edit still goes through the gate A domain expert may write in a UI, as long as that edit becomes a draft the same gate tests.
The registry is off the hot path Services read a local cache with a fallback, so a registry outage isn't a product outage.

In practice, OpenAI's guide (as of Oct 2026) says "treat prompts as application code", and its hosted v1/prompts shuts down on 30 Nov 2026. That argues against a store outside your release process, not against the hybrid.

Evolution

Lineage:2020–22 prompts as string literalsby 2024 hosted registriesJun 2025 OpenAI reusable promptsJun 2026 OpenAI deprecates them for prompts in code
  • Maturity: 🟡 Maturing (Oct 2026). Both positions are in wide use, with vendors on each side, so the choice is still argued.
  • Stronger-model test: no. The question is about your release process and who edits. What won't change: text that defines behaviour needs a test boundary somewhere.

Code

The hybrid's publish rule: only this job holds the registry's write token.

on: { push: { branches: [main], paths: ["prompts/**", "golden/**"] } }
jobs:
  publish:
    steps:
      - run: python -m prompts.render_all      # a missing slot fails here, with no model call
      - run: python -m evals.gate              # the contract cases block on one failure
      - run: python -m registry.publish --label staging
        env: { REGISTRY_WRITE_TOKEN: "${{ secrets.REGISTRY_WRITE_TOKEN }}" }

Decision rule: a version exists only if this job passed. Who may move production afterwards is governance.

Measure it

  • Offline: for the code path, the regression suite on every change; for the config path, the same suite against the version the label will point at, compared with the live version.
  • In production: served versions with no passing CI run (target zero), registry fetch errors, and time from a reported wrong line to the fix going live.
  • Enforced by: the write token held only by CI, and a regression gate on that path.

Interview

30-second answer: In code, the prompt ships in the build, gets review, and always matches its parser. In a registry, it changes without a deploy and non-engineers can edit it. The axis is who holds the pen and whether a prompt must release faster than code. I usually land on both: the repo as source, CI as the only publisher, and humans moving labels. A registry with no gate only makes bad changes faster.

Q · Mechanism — If the prompt lives in a database, what exactly have you lost? The guarantee that the prompt you tested is the prompt you serve, and the atomicity of a release. A code change and a prompt change that must land together travel on different channels, with no moment when both have happened. So output-contract changes ship as a new prompt name with a coordinated cutover, not as a new version of the old one.

Q · Trade-off — OpenAI is deleting its hosted prompts. Does that end the debate? No. The simpler rung is files in Git, and for one engineering team that's the answer. OpenAI's guide lists what you gain in code: review, tests, versioning, your own flags for rollout. It says nothing against a registry your CI publishes to. A second channel earns its cost when non-engineers edit or deploys are slower than your rollback target. If neither holds, stay on files.

Compare

In code In a registry Hybrid
Release with the deploy independent independent, tested
Rollback a deploy a pointer move a pointer move
Who edits engineers anyone with access anyone, through the gate
Serves what CI tested yes not by itself yes, by construction
Runtime dependency none the registry the registry, cached

Pitfalls

  • "A registry makes prompts managed, so they're safer"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: a UI with versions and roles looks like a control.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: decoupling prompt release from code release also decouples it from the test suite. Without a gate on publish, the registry is less safe than a repo.
    ↳ Think instead: the gate is the safety property; the registry is only a channel.
  • Not the same: where a prompt is authored vs where it's resolved
    ↳ Why they get mixed up: each tool's page covers both, so they read as one choice.
    ↳ Difference: authoring is about review and who edits. Resolving is about when the string is fixed, and so what could have changed it.
    ↳ Think instead: choose them separately: authored in the repo and resolved at run time is a valid pair.
  • Don't put an output contract in runtime config.
    ↳ Why it's tempting: it's one prompt among many in the same store.
    ↳ What goes wrong: an edit breaks downstream parsing with no build step in between, and only a production alert catches it.
    ↳ Do instead: keep contract-bearing prompts with their parser, or ship a new name with a cutover.
  • Don't climb to a platform for one prompt.
    ↳ Why it's tempting: registries are well marketed, and "no deploy" sounds free.
    ↳ What goes wrong: you add a critical dependency to win a speed nobody asked for.
    ↳ Do instead: use the simpler rung, files in Git with a flag or a versioned JSON file, until a real editor or a real deadline needs more.
  • Shelf life: the axis is durable. Vendor positions aren't: OpenAI's store goes away on 30 Nov 2026 (chapter map, Landscape).

Connections

Path:the prompt as a coupled systemcode vs configprompt versioningdecoupled release
  • Builds on prompt templating: typed slots decide whether a prompt can be config at all.
  • Measured by regression suites and CI: the gate that makes the config path defensible.
  • Costed in build vs buy: whether to run the registry yourself.
  • Drilled in prompts as code or config.

notes.title: Prompt Versioning — An Immutable Id the Trace Carries, a Movable Label the Service Reads
notes.html:
References

Langfuse: prompt management concepts · Langfuse: prompt version control · Braintrust: environments · OpenAI: migrate from prompt objects · Chip Huyen: building a generative AI platform

TL;DR

A version never changes; a label is a pointer you can move. The service reads the label, and the trace records the version. So shipping and rolling back are pointer moves, and any metric can be grouped by the exact text that produced it. A version proves nothing by existing: the gate in front of publish does that.

Stage:decidewriteassemblecallshapeevaluateshipwatchevery change
Flow:editrender and linteval gateappend v17, immutablemove staging, then productionservice resolves the labeltrace logs v17metrics per version

Recall

Prompt Answer
Version vs label? A version never changes; a label is a movable pointer to one.
What does the service name? A label online; a pinned version for eval and batch runs.
What must reach every trace? The resolved version, not the label: the label hides what ran.
When is a new version not enough? An output-contract change: new name, coordinated cutover with the parser.
Draw by hand: the version pipeline Edit → gate → append version → labels ← service; trace logs version → metrics → gate.
What still holds if the model ignores the prompt? Attribution: the record says what was sent, whatever came back.

The idea

Quality dropped on Tuesday. Five prompts changed in that release, and the logs say prompt=refund-extractor. You can line a chart up with a deploy window, and that's all you can do. The investigation has no edges.

Now give every saved edit an id that is never reused, and stamp that id into each request's trace. "Quality dropped" becomes "v17 fails to parse 12% of the time and v16 doesn't". Move the pointer back and the same binary serves v16.

You may think Git already does this. Git gives you history, review and diffs, which is most of the value and enough for many teams. What versioning adds is an id that survives into telemetry. A commit SHA qualifies only if you stamp it into the trace, and a whole-repo SHA changes for unrelated edits, so a content hash of the rendered template is the sharper id.

This is enforced, not requested: the model plays no part. The tuple around the prompt (model, settings, parser) is owned by the prompt as a coupled system. This note is how one member of it gets an address.

The trade: an id on every trace and a pointer layer cost a small amount of machinery; without them every prompt incident starts as an unbounded search.

How it works

One append-only log, one mutable layer, and a loop back through the traces.

Only the label layer moves. Everything left of it is history, and history is what makes an old trace readable.

Rule What actually happens
Never edit a version in place A trace from three weeks ago must still mean the same text. An edit makes every old trace point at words that never ran.
Serving reads a label; reproducing pins a version Online, the pointer is what lets you roll back. In an eval or a batch job, a pointer that moves mid-run ruins the comparison.
The name is the interface Same name means same output contract. A new schema is a new name, shipped with its parser, because a label move can't be atomic with code.
Log what ran, not what you asked for The label says what was requested. Under a traffic split it stays the same while two versions run.
A version change is a cache change An edit near the top of the prompt moves the prefix, so cache hits fall on the promotion. Expect it in the cost line.

Evolution

Lineage:2020–22 string literals in codeJan 2024 Langfuse ships prompt versions, labels followJun 2025 OpenAI reusable prompts in the APIJun 2026 OpenAI deprecates them for prompts in code
  • Maturity: 🟢 Established (Oct 2026). Registries and evaluation platforms converge on versions plus pointers (chapter map, Landscape). Where the versions live is the part still moving.
  • Stronger-model test: no. A better model changes how much a version matters, not whether you can tell two apart. What won't change: a metric can only be grouped by an id that was logged.

Code

The record for one version, with the mutable part kept apart.

name: refund-extractor               # the interface: one output contract
version: 17                          # never reused, never edited
content_hash: "sha256:…"             # of template + settings, computed in CI
source: prompts/refund_extract.md@4e1d2b0
output_schema: refund.v3             # a change here means a new name
model: "{{pinned model snapshot}}"
settings: { effort: medium, max_tokens: 400 }
passed: { eval_set: golden/refund@v9, run: ci-8412 }
# stored separately, and the only thing that moves:
labels: { staging: 17, production: 16 }

Break it: one label in the log, two versions behind it, a tenth of traffic on the new one.

from collections import defaultdict
log = [("production", 16, i % 200 == 0) for i in range(900)] \
    + [("production", 17, i % 9 == 0) for i in range(100)]    # (label, version, failed)
def rate(key):
    n, f = defaultdict(int), defaultdict(int)
    for label, ver, failed in log:
        n[key(label, ver)] += 1; f[key(label, ver)] += failed
    return {k: round(f[k] / n[k], 3) for k in n}
print(rate(lambda label, ver: label)); print(rate(lambda label, ver: ver))
# look for: one blended rate when grouped by label, two very different rates by version
# naive belief predicts: logging the label is enough to see a bad canary

Run on Python 3.15, it prints {'production': 0.017}, then {16: 0.006, 17: 0.12}. The label's line looks healthy while the canary fails one call in eight. PromptLayer's docs warn of this for its traffic splits: the label in your logs stays the original, so log the version returned.

Measure it

  • Offline: every version in the log links to a passing run against the regression suite; the baseline is the version it replaces, on the same set version.
  • In production: the share of traces with a resolved version id, target 100%. Then parse failure, refusals and cost per version, and distinct versions live per day.
  • Enforced by: CI, as the only identity allowed to publish, and an append-only store. Code writes the trace field, in one client library, so no team has to remember it.

Interview

30-second answer: Every prompt edit creates an immutable version, and the service resolves a label like production that points at one. Promotion and rollback become pointer moves. The resolved version goes into every trace, so I can say v17 dropped parse rate, not that quality fell on Tuesday. The gotcha is that versioning proves nothing by itself: without a gate before publish, it just ships untested text faster.

Q · Mechanism — Isn't Git already prompt versioning? It's most of it: history, review and diffs, and for one team on frequent deploys that's the right answer. Two gaps remain. Your telemetry must carry an id, so stamp a content hash or commit into the trace at build time. And a Git-only rollback takes a deploy; if that's too slow, add a pointer layer. OpenAI's own guidance is now the Git side of this, with rollout through your feature flags.

Q · Trade-off — Should the service pin a version or resolve a label? The simpler rung is a pin in code: the pod serves exactly what its config says, and a rollback is a deploy. That's right for batch jobs and eval runs, where reproducibility is the point. Online, the label buys rollback without a build, at the price of a window where the fleet serves two versions, which decoupled release measures. That's harmless for tone and unacceptable for anything a parser reads.

Q · Failure — A prompt change degraded a feature and nobody noticed for three days. What happened? Attribution failed, not storage. Confirm by asking whether the traces carry a resolved version, and whether any metric is grouped by it. Usually a blended rate moved a little and no one could tie it to a change. Fix the trace schema first. Then compare each promotion with the previous version's rolling baseline on parse failures and refusals, and wire that alert to a label revert.

Q · Design — Design versioning for 3,000 versions across 50 services. The binding constraint is inventory, not storage: nobody can say which version a tenant is on. So label-to-version mappings are data, snapshotted on a schedule, and an incident starts from a diff. Prompts live in repos with fixtures; CI publishes; one thin client library resolves labels, caches, falls back when the registry is down, and writes the trace field. Promotion is a separate, governed act. I'd watch the share of untraced requests first. It sits in the prompt-layer reference architecture.

Compare

Immutable version Movable label Commit SHA alone
Changes over time never yes, by design never
The service names it in eval and batch runs online not at run time
Reaches the trace must as context only if stamped
Rollback change config, deploy move the pointer revert, deploy

Numbers

Number Value Context Source
Blended failure rate 1.7% 90% of traffic at about 0.6%, 10% at 12% derived, and measured in Break it
Traces needed to attribute a change all of them a request with no version belongs to no group derived

Pitfalls

  • "Versioning means keeping a history of prompt strings"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: the visible feature of every tool is a list of old versions with a diff.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: a history nobody joins to production answers no question. Without the id in the trace, you still can't say which version caused a drop.
    ↳ Think instead: the valuable half is addressability: one id, in every trace.
  • "A new version is compatible, it's just wording"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: a diff of two lines looks smaller than any code change.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: a prompt has an implicit interface: the shape its consumers parse. A tone edit that adds a sentence before the JSON takes down a service that never changed.
    ↳ Think instead: same name, same contract; a new contract gets a new name.
  • "Moving prompts into a registry made them safer"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: "managed" sounds like a control, and the UI looks like one.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: I had taken prompts off the path that ran the tests. A registry with no gate is a faster way to ship an unmeasured string.
    ↳ Think instead: the registry is a channel; the gate is the control.
  • Not the same: a prompt version vs a model version
    ↳ Why they get mixed up: dashboards often show a single "version" field.
    ↳ Difference: you decide when a prompt version changes. The provider decides when a model snapshot is withdrawn, and a default it changes can move behaviour too.
    ↳ Think instead: log both separately, and derive the tuple id from both.
  • Don't add a registry for one team on daily deploys.
    ↳ Why it's tempting: it's the architecture in every platform diagram.
    ↳ What goes wrong: you buy a runtime dependency and a second copy of the truth to win rollback seconds you don't need.
    ↳ Do instead: prompts in files, a content hash in the trace, Git and a flag. Climb when non-engineers edit or a deploy is slower than your rollback target.
  • "We log the prompts, so we can audit anything"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: full text feels like the complete record.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: rendered prompts hold user data, so storing them all creates a retention and access problem, and they still don't group into metrics without the id.
    ↳ Think instead: ids for every request, text for a redacted sample, as prompt observability splits them.
  • Shelf life: immutable ids and movable pointers are durable. Which product holds them isn't: one provider's hosted store shuts down on 30 Nov 2026 (chapter map, Landscape).

Connections

Path:the prompt as a coupled systemcode vs configprompt versioningdecoupled releaseprompt observability
  • Builds on the prompt as a coupled system: it owns the tuple; this note gives the prompt its address.
  • Measured by regression suites and CI: the gate a version passes before it exists.
  • Owned elsewhere: versioning and rollout (LLM-Production) covers the platform view across prompts, models and retrieval.
  • Used by model-upgrade migration: holding the prompt fixed needs an addressable prompt.
  • Enforced by prompt governance: who may move production.
  • Drilled in decoupling prompt releases.

notes.title: Prompt Registries & Tooling — Same Primitives, Different Starting Point
notes.html:
References

Langfuse: prompt management · PromptLayer: release labels

TL;DR

Registries share a small set of primitives: immutable versions, movable labels and links to traces. Choose by deployment model and by what you already run. Products and owners change quickly, so the dated list lives in the chapter map's Landscape.

Stage:decidewriteassemblecallshapeevaluateshipwatchevery change

Recall

Prompt Answer
The shared primitives? Immutable versions, movable labels, diffs, per-version metrics joined to traces.
How do you choose? Self-hosting needs, then whether tracing or evals should share the tool.
What did 2025–26 teach? Stores close and change hands, so export must be cheap: keep the repo as source.

The idea

You're asked which registry to use. Comparing feature lists gets you nowhere, because they converged. The tools differ in where they started: Langfuse from open-source tracing, PromptLayer from release labels, Braintrust from evals, LaunchDarkly from feature flags. Promptfoo is a test runner, not a store. Humanloop shut down in 2025, and OpenAI's hosted prompts stop on 30 Nov 2026. A store you don't own can vanish, so author in the repo.

Evolution

By 2024 hosted registries ─▶ 2025–26 consolidation: Humanloop, Langfuse and Promptfoo acquired. 🟡 Maturing (Oct 2026): the primitives settled, the vendors haven't.

notes.title: Decoupling Prompt Release from Code Release — Rollback Is a Pointer Move Plus Propagation
notes.html:
References

Langfuse: prompt caching · PromptLayer: dynamic release labels · LaunchDarkly: AgentControl targeting · OpenAI: migrate from prompt objects

TL;DR

The service resolves a label, so releasing a prompt is moving that label and rolling back is moving it back, with no build. The move itself takes seconds. Rollback takes as long as your slowest cached copy. Under stale-while-revalidate that's the next request after the TTL, however late it comes. Cohorts are chosen outside the prompt, per user, so you can ramp up and back.

Stage:decidewriteassemblecallshapeevaluateshipwatchevery change
Flow:tested v17canary label, 5% by usercompare with v16, same windowrampmove productioncaches refresh
drop the canaryusers stay on v16

Recall

Prompt Answer
The mechanism in one word? Indirection: the app resolves a label, and you repoint it.
Rollback time equals? The move plus cache propagation; never just the API call.
What must not ship this way? Anything a downstream parser depends on: an output-contract change.

The idea

A prompt change broke something at 4 pm. In code, the fix is a revert, a build and a rolling restart, so recovery time equals deploy time.

With a pointer, the same binary serves the old version as soon as the pointer moves and the caches catch up. The value is recovery time, more than convenience for whoever edits prompts: daily releases are defensible because the way back is short.

Split the pointer by cohort, and 5% of users see v17 while the rest stay on v16. The prompt knows nothing about who's getting it; the resolution layer does.

The trade: you recover without a deploy, and your fleet serves two versions during every move, so anything atomic with code can't use this path.

How it works

Every version goes through the same states, and only code moves it between them.

Decision rule: a step ramps only if the new version is no worse than the old one in the same window, on the same cohort rules. A rise in parse failures or refusals beyond the noise stops it, whatever a judged score says. Comparing user behaviour is an A/B test, which owns the sample size.

Rule What actually happens
Assign by user or session, and keep it A user who flips between versions mid-conversation sees incoherent behaviour, and pollutes both versions' metrics.
Log what was served A split label reads as one version in logs, so record the resolved version.
Know your cache's policy With stale-while-revalidate, an expired entry is returned once more, then refreshed.

Evolution

Lineage:2010s feature flags and canaries for codeJan 2024 hosted prompt versions, then labelsby 2026 flag platforms and registries split prompt traffic by percentage
  • Maturity: 🟢 Established (Oct 2026). Registries and a flag platform all ship staged rollout for prompts.
  • Stronger-model test: no. A stronger model breaks less often, and each release still needs a way back. What won't change: a cached copy lags its source.

Code

The rollout rule, kept as data so a promotion is a reviewable change.

prompt: refund-extractor
from: 16
to: 17                    # must already exist, so it already passed the gate
assign_by: user_id        # sticky: one person sees one version
steps: [5, 25, 50, 100]   # percent of users
hold_each_step: 2h
stop_if_worse:
  - parse_failure_rate    # compared with v16 in the same window
  - refusal_rate
on_stop: revert_label     # automatic: no meeting at 4 pm

Break it: a rollback against two pods on a stale-while-revalidate cache, one busy and one quiet.

class Pod:
    def __init__(s, reg, ttl): s.reg, s.ttl, s.val, s.at = reg, ttl, reg["production"], 0
    def get(s, t):                                  # stale-while-revalidate
        out = s.val                                 # the caller gets the cached value at once
        if t - s.at >= s.ttl:                       # expired: refresh for the NEXT caller
            s.val, s.at = s.reg["production"], t
        return out
reg = {"production": "v17"}
busy, quiet = Pod(reg, 60), Pod(reg, 60)
reg["production"] = "v16"                           # rollback at t=120; pods fetched v17 at t=0
print([busy.get(t) for t in (121, 122)], [quiet.get(t) for t in (3600, 3601)])
# look for: the quiet pod serving v17 an hour after the rollback
# naive belief predicts: every pod is on v16 within one 60-second TTL of the move

Run on Python 3.15, it prints ['v17', 'v16'] ['v17', 'v16']. The quiet pod's first caller an hour later still got the bad version: the TTL allows a refresh, it doesn't cause one. For a hard limit, refresh on a timer.

Measure it

  • Offline: before any traffic, the new version against the live one on the same golden set, by the regression gate. A canary doesn't replace it.
  • In production: per version in one window: parse failures, refusals, output length. Also rollback time measured end to end: label moved to last process serving the old version.
  • Enforced by: the rollout controller that reverts on a stopped metric, and the label protection that keeps people off it.

Interview

30-second answer: The service resolves a label, so shipping is moving it and rolling back is moving it back, with no deploy. Cohorts sit outside the prompt, so I can ramp by user. The cost is two versions running during a move, fine for tone and fatal for output contracts. And rollback time is propagation, not the API call.

Q · Mechanism — You get instant rollback but lose "ship what CI tested". How do you get both? Let only CI publish, and let people only move labels, so the fastest panic move points at something tested. Evals still aren't production: a version can pass and regress live, so the rollout is staged and compared with the previous version in the same window.

Q · Trade-off — When isn't decoupling worth it? The simpler rung is Git plus a redeploy, the honest choice for one team with quick deploys. Climb when deploy time exceeds your target for fixing a bad prompt, or when non-engineers release. Long cache lifetimes kept to save fetches buy you less recovery time than you think.

Numbers

Number Value Context Source
Langfuse SDK default cache lifetime 60 s then stale-while-revalidate; cache_ttl_seconds sets it cited (volatile, as of Oct 2026)
Worst-case staleness under that policy no bound until the process's next request after expiry derived, and measured in Break it

Pitfalls

  • "Rollback is instant"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: the label move really does take a moment, and the demo stops there.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: every process keeps serving its cached copy, a quiet one long after the TTL (Break it).
    ↳ Think instead: quote the measured time to the last process, not the API call.
  • Not the same: a canary vs an A/B test
    ↳ Why they get mixed up: both split traffic between two versions behind the same label.
    ↳ Difference: a canary asks whether it's safe to continue, ramps up, and stops on a worse signal. An A/B test asks whether users behaved differently, with a fixed split and end date.
    ↳ Think instead: run the canary to limit damage, and the A/B test to decide on value.
  • Don't ship an output-contract change on a label.
    ↳ Why it's tempting: it's the same button as every other release.
    ↳ What goes wrong: during the move, new prompts meet old parsers, and no ordering of the two avoids it.
    ↳ Do instead: a new prompt name, read by a parser that handles both shapes, with a planned cutover.
  • Don't build a rollout controller for a prompt that rarely changes.
    ↳ Why it's tempting: automatic revert is the mature picture.
    ↳ What goes wrong: you run cohorts and dashboards for a change made twice a year.
    ↳ Do instead: the simpler rung: a deploy behind the suite, until prompt changes outpace deploys.
  • Shelf life: indirection and sticky assignment are durable. Defaults and product names aren't: LaunchDarkly's AI Configs are now called AgentControl (chapter map, Landscape).

Connections

Path:prompt versioningdecoupled releasemulti-tenant promptsprompt observability
  • Builds on prompt versioning: versions are what labels point at.
  • Measured by regression suites and CI before traffic, prompt observability during it.
  • Owned elsewhere: versioning and rollout (LLM-Production) covers canaries across the whole bundle.
  • Enforced by prompt governance: if anyone can move production, the gate is advice.
  • Drilled in decoupling prompt releases.

notes.title: Model-Upgrade Migration — Make the Request Valid, Hold the Prompt, Measure, Then Tune
notes.html:
References

Anthropic: model deprecations · Anthropic: Opus 5.5 migration guide · OpenAI: deprecations · Google: Gemini deprecations

TL;DR

A model swap isn't a config change: your prompt was fitted to the old model, and the provider can retire that model on its own clock. So work in order: make the request validsame prompt on both modelstriage by what each output reachestune only what regressed. Change the model or the prompt in one comparison, never both.
Stage:decidewriteassemblecallshapeevaluateshipwatchevery change
Flow:retirement datelint requests against the new modelsame prompt, both models, golden setper-prompt deltamodel field only
tune a new versionre-runcanary per prompt

Recall

Prompt Answer
What breaks first on a new model? The request: removed parameters and prefill return errors before quality is measured.
What do you hold fixed? The prompt, while the model changes; then the model, while the prompt changes.
How do you scope the work? By blast radius: parsed or deciding outputs first, human-read drafts last.

The idea

Your provider emails a retirement date. You change the model id, and the extraction service returns 400s: the request sets temperature: 0 and ends in an assistant prefill, and the new model accepts neither. You remove them, and the golden set shows a drop. Was it the model, or the prefill you took away?

So first make the request valid, with the smallest change you can. Then run one prompt version on both models and write down a table: same set, per-metric delta, per prompt. Only the rows that regressed get prompt work.

The coupled-system note owns why; this note owns the procedure.

The trade: an eval run per prompt costs real money, and it replaces one risky cutover with decisions you can defend.

How it works

Two gates before any edit: does it run, and did it get worse?

Decision rule: a prompt moves when no contract case fails and no tracked metric falls beyond the noise, by the regression gate. Any rise in failures on a parsed prompt blocks; a small delta on a human-read draft may be accepted, in writing.

Rule What actually happens
Settings are part of the swap As of Oct 2026 all three major providers are narrowing or removing sampling parameters (chapter map, Landscape). A temperature may be a 400, a warning or ignored.
Defaults move without an edit On Anthropic's models, Opus 5's default effort is high and Opus 5.5's is medium. A request that omits it changes behaviour silently. Set it, and sweep it.
Re-derive compensations Anthropic's guide says instructions tuned for the previous model "might no longer be needed". Measure the removal; don't assume it.
Migrate per prompt With the model in each prompt's config, each one moves through a canary alone.

Evolution

Lineage:2023 dated snapshots such as gpt-4-03142024–25 reasoning models change what prompts need2026 sampling settings removed or ignored on new modelsOct 2026 Anthropic API version 2026-10-21 rejects them on every model
  • Maturity: 🟢 Established (Oct 2026). Every provider publishes retirements and notice periods, so migration is routine work.
  • Stronger-model test: no: each one is itself the event. What won't change: only a measured table says which prompts to touch.
  • Checked on: provider guides for Claude 5.5, GPT-6 and Gemini 3.x, read Oct 2026; none gives a measured regression rate.

Code

The migration's deliverable is a table, one record per prompt.

prompt: refund-extractor
version: 17                  # held fixed across both runs
models: { from: "{{old snapshot}}", to: "{{new snapshot}}" }
eval_set: golden/refund@v9
request_changes: [temperature removed, prefill to schema, effort set]
delta: { contract_failures: "{{n}}", judged: "{{± noise}}", cost_per_success: "{{%}}" }
reaches: parser
decision: model_field_only   # or: tune | accept

Break it: the belief that a model change can only affect quality. This lint needs no API call.

REJECTS = {"old": set(), "new": {"temperature", "top_p", "top_k", "prefill"}}  # dated rules
def lint(req, model):
    used = set(req) - {"messages"}
    if req["messages"][-1]["role"] == "assistant": used.add("prefill")
    return sorted(used & REJECTS[model])
req = {"temperature": 0, "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "{{doc}}"},
                                      {"role": "assistant", "content": "{"}]}
print("old:", lint(req, "old")); print("new:", lint(req, "new"))
# look for: an empty list on the old model, two rejected fields on the new one
# naive belief predicts: the same request is accepted, and only its quality can differ

Run on Python 3.15, it prints old: [], then new: ['prefill', 'temperature']. A stored request shows its breakages before any tokens are spent.

Measure it

  • Offline: per prompt, a freshly resampled golden set on both models, prompt held fixed, as paired differences; plus cost and tokens re-baselined.
  • In production: requests still on the old model per prompt, counting down to the date; then parse failures, refusals and cost per success by model.
  • Enforced by: the regression gate on the tuple, and the provider's date, which turns unmigrated requests into errors.

Interview

30-second answer: A prompt is fitted to one model, so an upgrade re-baselines it. First I make requests valid, because parameters and prefill may be rejected. Then I freeze the prompt, run the golden set on both models, and tune only what regressed and matters. Migration runs per prompt through a canary, so a retirement date isn't one cutover.

Q · Mechanism — Why not point the same prompt at the new model and ship? Because the prompt holds compensations for the old model, and only measuring shows which still matter. Examples that steadied a format, or a reasoning preamble, may now cost tokens or change results. So you build the table: same set, same prompt, both models.

Q · Trade-off — The old model retires in eight weeks. Tune everything? No. The simpler rung is the model field alone, and the table says where that's enough. Parsed outputs and decisions get real prompt work and a staged rollout; human-read drafts can absorb a small recorded delta. Tuning everything before measuring wastes the window.

Numbers

Number Value Context Source
Notice before a retirement at least 60 days Anthropic, publicly released models cited (volatile, as of Oct 2026)
Notice before a shutdown at least 6 months; 3 for specialised variants; about 2 weeks for previews OpenAI's stated policy cited (volatile, as of Oct 2026)

Pitfalls

  • "A newer model with the same prompt can only improve things"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: benchmarks rise with every release, and the announcement says so.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: those are averages over someone else's tasks. Your prompt's format and examples were selected on the old model.
    ↳ Think instead: better on average can be worse on your prompt: run the table.
  • Don't tune in the same change as the swap.
    ↳ Why it's tempting: with a deadline, doing both feels efficient.
    ↳ What goes wrong: a result moves and you can't attribute it, so obsolete compensations stay.
    ↳ Do instead: make the minimum request edits, swap and measure, then tune as a separate version.
  • Don't migrate just because a newer model exists.
    ↳ Why it's tempting: the latest model feels like staying current.
    ↳ What goes wrong: the eval costs money, and a healthy prompt can regress for no gain.
    ↳ Do instead: stay on the simpler rung until a date, a price or a measured gap gives you a reason.
  • Not the same: a retired model vs a moved alias
    ↳ Why they get mixed up: both change what your requests reach without any edit from you.
    ↳ Difference: retirement turns a pinned id into errors. An alias such as gemini-flash-latest silently serves a different model, with 2 weeks' notice for breaking changes (as of Oct 2026).
    ↳ Think instead: pin a snapshot in production, and treat an alias as a tuple that changes without your commit.
  • Shelf life: the order of work is durable. The rules of what's rejected, and every date above, change with each model (chapter map, Landscape).

Connections

Path:the prompt as a coupled systemprompt versioningmodel-upgrade migrationdecoupled release
  • Builds on the prompt as a coupled system: why a model bump is a tuple change.
  • Measured by regression suites and CI: the suite is the triage tool.
  • Contrasts with portability of optimised prompts: there you re-compile; here you re-measure by hand.
  • Used by model-family differences: the per-family facts that feed the lint rules.
  • Drilled in a model upgrade regressed the prompts.

notes.title: Multi-tenant & Localised Prompts — One Template, N Validated Config Rows
notes.html:
References

Langfuse: prompt version control · LaunchDarkly: AgentControl targeting · OpenAI: migrate from prompt objects · Shi et al. 2022: multilingual chain-of-thought

TL;DR

Four hundred tenants don't need four hundred prompts. Fork the variables, not the prompt: one versioned template with typed slots, and one validated config row per tenant. That's one artifact to migrate, and the bill is eval coverage: 400 configs are still 400 behaviours. A tenant-editable slot sits inside your instructions, so it's untrusted input. Validate it before it renders.

Stage:decidewriteassemblecallshapeevaluateshipwatchevery change
Flow:request with tenant and localeresolve the template by labelload tenant and locale configvalidate against the schemarender with static text firstcalllog version, config version, tenant, locale

─fail─▶ reject and alert, never render a partial prompt

Recall

Prompt Answer
The rule in one line? Fork the variables, never the prompt: one template, N config rows.
What forces a real second template? A structurally different prompt: a product decision, not a tenant tweak.
How does eval survive 400 tenants? Shared core suite for all; a small smoke suite per config change.

The idea

Each customer wants a tweak, so someone copies the prompt: support_acme, support_bolt, and so on. A year later a fix to the injection guard needs 400 edits, and some get missed.

Now keep one template and turn what differs into typed slots: tone, glossary, forbidden topics, locale. The fix ships once. The upgrade is measured once, with a smaller check per tenant. A config row can be validated and diffed, which a forked paragraph can't.

The trade: one template concentrates risk and needs a schema and tiered evals; forks feel free and charge you on every later change.

How it works

Resolution is an ordered path with one hard stop.

The stop is the point: a failed slot must fail loudly, or the prompt renders with a hole no test covered.

Rule What actually happens
Typed slots, closed where possible An enum for tone and a schema name for output leave nothing to inject. Free text gets a length cap, and it's treated as data, not instructions.
Tenant text after the static prefix A tenant line at the top changes the prefix for everyone (Break it), so cache hits vanish.
Tiered evals Template change: core suite plus each tier's smoke cases. Config change: that tenant's smoke cases. Which suite runs when is owned by regression suites and CI.
Language: keep the scaffold, swap the content Default to one instruction language with a locale slot for output. Where wording is the content (legal text, a register, a glossary), inject translated slots into that scaffold.

Per-locale forks are the last resort: each one needs its own golden set, and that's where localisation budgets go. Cross-lingual prompting owns instruction language against content language.

Evolution

Lineage:SaaS per-tenant config2024 prompt labels per environmentby 2026 labels and targeting rules per tenant and segment
  • Maturity: 🟢 Established (Oct 2026). Ordinary multi-tenant design applied to text; Langfuse lists tenants among its label uses.
  • Stronger-model test: no. A model that handles languages better shrinks the locale problem, and four hundred forks still cost four hundred fixes. What won't change: one artifact is cheaper to change than many.
  • Checked on: Shi et al. showed chain-of-thought reasoning across languages on MGSM with 2022 models. That doesn't prove your prompt transfers, so keep locale cases in the set.

Code

One tenant row, and the schema that gates it.

tenant: acme
template: support-agent        # resolved by label; this row names no version
tier: enterprise
tone: formal                   # enum: formal | neutral | casual
glossary: glossaries/acme@v4   # reviewed data, capped in length
forbidden_topics: [legal-advice, competitors]   # closed list
output_schema: support.v3      # must exist; a new schema is a new template
locale: de-DE                  # sets output language and formats

Break it: the same template rendered for two tenants, with the tenant line at the top and then at the bottom.

STATIC = "You classify support tickets. Labels: billing, bug, how-to, other. " * 40
A, B = "Tenant: Acme. Tone: formal.\n", "Tenant: Bolt. Tone: casual.\n"
def shared(x, y):
    return next((i for i, (a, b) in enumerate(zip(x, y)) if a != b), min(len(x), len(y)))
print("tenant first:", shared(A + STATIC, B + STATIC), "of", len(A + STATIC))
print("tenant last: ", shared(STATIC + A, STATIC + B), "of", len(STATIC + A))
# look for: how many characters of the prompt two tenants share as a prefix
# naive belief predicts: the same long shared prefix, since only one line differs

Run on Python 3.15, it prints tenant first: 8 of 2708, then tenant last: 2688 of 2708. One line in the wrong place leaves two tenants sharing 8 characters, so no prefix cache can serve them both.

Measure it

  • Offline: the core suite on any template change, against the live version, plus each tier's smoke cases; on a config change, that tenant's cases against its previous config.
  • In production: parse failures and refusals per tenant and locale, rendered-prompt hashes per config version, cache-read share per tenant, and schema rejections.
  • Enforced by: the schema check before render, closed enums, and the label scope. An instruction to respect a tenant's forbidden topics is a request; an output check is what enforces it.

Interview

30-second answer: I keep one versioned template with typed slots, and each tenant is a validated config row: one artifact to migrate, plus data I can diff. Labels scope rollout by tier. The cost is eval coverage, because 400 configs are 400 behaviours. A structurally different prompt is a new template and a product decision.

Q · Mechanism — Why is forking a prompt per tenant so bad? It's only text. Every fork must be evaluated, migrated and debugged on its own. It also destroys your signal: with one template, a regression across tenants points at the template; with forks, each tenant is a population too small to say anything.

Q · Trade-off — Translate the prompt, or instruct the output language? The simpler rung is one instruction language plus a locale slot: fixes reach every locale at once. It stops being enough where the content is locale-specific: regulated wording, a formality register, terms with no clean translation. Then inject translated slots into the same scaffold.

Pitfalls

  • "Per-tenant prompts mean per-tenant versions"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: a tenant's behaviour changed, so something must have a new version.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: config changes far more often than the template. Mixing them floods the version log and hides the template edits you care about.
    ↳ Think instead: two lifecycles: one template version, N config versions, both logged.
  • Don't render unvalidated tenant text inside your instructions.
    ↳ Why it's tempting: it's a customer's own configuration, so it feels trusted.
    ↳ What goes wrong: a slot holding free text is an injection path wearing a config label, and a bad slot can also render a broken prompt silently.
    ↳ Do instead: closed enums where you can, length caps and review for free text, and a request-time schema check.
  • Don't build a slot system for two tenants.
    ↳ Why it's tempting: you can see the four-hundredth tenant from here.
    ↳ What goes wrong: you maintain a schema, a config store and tier suites for one conditional's worth of difference.
    ↳ Do instead: the simpler rung: two config rows and a conditional, until the third request arrives.
  • Not the same: a config row vs a structural difference
    ↳ Why they get mixed up: both start as "this customer needs something else".
    ↳ Difference: a row fills the same slots. A different schema or task breakdown changes the shape, and forcing it into slots fills the template with mutually exclusive conditionals.
    ↳ Think instead: if a change needs a new conditional branch, ask whether it's a new template.
  • Shelf life: the fork rule and the two lifecycles are durable. Tool support for targeting changes quickly (chapter map, Landscape).

Connections

Path:prompt templatingprompt versioningdecoupled releasemulti-tenant promptsprompt observability
  • Builds on prompt templating: typed slots are its mechanism.
  • Attacked by indirect prompt injection: a tenant-supplied slot is untrusted text in the window.
  • Owned elsewhere: API-level multi-tenancy (LLM-Production) covers quotas and rate limits.
  • Breaks when combined with cache ordering if tenant text comes first.
  • Drilled in four hundred tenants and works in English, fails elsewhere.

notes.title: Prompt Observability — One Cheap Record per Call, Joined on the Version
notes.html:
References

OpenTelemetry: GenAI semantic conventions · Langfuse: prompt management · Chip Huyen: building a generative AI platform

TL;DR

From one call, write two records: a small metrics record for every request, and a text record, sampled, redacted and short-lived. The resolved version id is the join key. With it, "quality dropped Tuesday" becomes "v17 regressed parse rate on one tier". Most prompt regressions show up in signals you already have, with no judge model: parse failures, refusals, truncation, output length.

Stage:decidewriteassemblecallshapeevaluateshipwatchevery request
Flow:callclient stamps name, version, label, hashmetrics record, all requestsrollups per version
redacted text record, short retentionjudge on the samplesame rollups ─worse than previous versionalert, revert label

Recall

Prompt Answer
The field that makes the rest work? The resolved prompt version id on every record.
The cheapest high-signal quality metric? Schema or parse failure rate; it needs no judge.
Why hash the rendered prompt too? Slots vary by tenant, so the hash catches config-side changes.

The idea

You log every prompt in full. A month later a security review asks why you hold customer text with no retention rule. When quality drops, you can search that archive but can't draw one line per version, because nothing joins the text to a release.

Split the job in two. A small record for every request holds ids, counts and outcomes: this is what you chart and alert on. A separate record holds the rendered prompt and output, for a redacted sample, with a short lifetime and its own access control.

The platform's traces, dashboards and pipelines are owned by LLM observability. This note covers the prompt-shaped fields.

The trade: two streams cost more design up front, and in return the signal you alert on carries no customer text.

How it works

Two streams from one call, joined on the version.

The left path is free and catches breakage. The right path costs model calls and measures quality, so it's sampled.

What you record Field (OpenTelemetry GenAI, status: Development, as of Oct 2026) What it catches
Which prompt gen_ai.prompt.name, gen_ai.prompt.version a change that moved a metric
Which model gen_ai.request.model, gen_ai.response.model a moved alias: the two differ
What it cost gen_ai.usage.input_tokens, gen_ai.usage.output_tokens a version that grew, or a cache that went cold
How it ended gen_ai.response.finish_reasons, plus your parse result truncation, refusals, broken JSON
The text gen_ai.input.messages, gen_ai.output.messages (opt-in) content review, on a sample only

Keep metric labels bounded: version, model, tenant tier and locale are safe. User ids and raw text belong in traces, or the metrics store's cardinality explodes.

Evolution

Lineage:May 2024 Langfuse compares metrics across prompt versionsJan 2025 OpenTelemetry post on GenAI conventions, in development2026 conventions move to their own repository, with prompt name and version attributes
  • Maturity: 🟡 Maturing (Oct 2026). The two-stream pattern is settled; the standard attributes are still marked Development and may be renamed.
  • Stronger-model test: no. A stronger model fails less often, and a release still needs a line per version. What won't change: you can only group by what you recorded.

Code

The metrics record, using the standard names, with your own fields kept under your namespace.

gen_ai.prompt.name: refund-extractor
gen_ai.prompt.version: "17"            # resolved, not the label
gen_ai.request.model: "{{pinned model snapshot}}"
gen_ai.usage.input_tokens: 1840
gen_ai.usage.output_tokens: 212
gen_ai.response.finish_reasons: [stop]
app.prompt.label: production           # context: what was asked for
app.prompt.rendered_hash: "sha256:…"   # moves when a tenant slot moves
app.tenant_tier: enterprise
app.parse_ok: true                     # the cheapest quality signal

Break it: the belief that a version with shorter output is cheaper. Rates are $2 and $10 per million input and output tokens, and failures are retried.

def per_success(input_t, output_t, success, rin=2.0, rout=10.0):
    call = (input_t * rin + output_t * rout) / 1e6
    return round(call, 6), round(call / success, 6)    # failed calls are billed too
print("v16", per_success(1000, 500, 0.98))
print("v17", per_success(1000, 400, 0.70))
# look for: which version is cheaper per call, and which per success
# naive belief predicts: v17 is cheaper, because it uses fewer tokens per call

Run on Python 3.15, it prints v16 (0.007, 0.007143), then v17 (0.006, 0.008571). v17 costs 14% less per call and 20% more per success. So chart cost per successful outcome, by version. The cost sum itself is owned by cost modelling.

Measure it

  • Offline: replay a stored sample through the logging path, and check every record has a version, a model and an outcome; the baseline is the schema, not a prompt.
  • In production: per version against the previous one in the same window: parse failures, refusals, finish reasons, output length, cost per success. Also the share of records with no version.
  • Enforced by: one client library that writes the fields, and redaction before the text store. A request that bypasses the library is the gap to alert on.

Interview

30-second answer: One record per call, with prompt name, resolved version, label, rendered hash, model, tenant and locale, tokens and outcome. That turns "quality dropped" into "v17 regressed parse rate on tier 3". The full text goes to a separate sampled, redacted, short-lived store. OpenTelemetry's GenAI conventions now name the prompt fields, though they're still marked Development. Most regressions show up in free signals before any judge.

Q · Mechanism — What do you log, and what do you deliberately not log? Always: the ids, the model, token counts, latency and outcome signals such as parse success and finish reason. Conditionally: the rendered prompt and completion, because they hold user data, so they get sampling, redaction, shorter retention and separate access control. The permanent record stays free of customer text.

Q · Trade-off — A judge on live traffic is expensive. How do you get an online quality signal? The simpler rung is free: parse failures, refusals, truncation and output length catch format and instruction-following regressions, and those need no model call. Add a judge when you need to see quality move while those stay flat. Run it on a sample stratified per live version, weighted to the active canary, so spend follows rollout risk. If the interval is too wide to separate two versions, raise the sample for that prompt only.

Pitfalls

  • "We log prompts, so we have prompt observability"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: full text feels like total visibility, and it's the first thing a tracing tool gives you.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: text with no version id is a searchable archive, not a metric. You can read one call, and you can't compare two releases.
    ↳ Think instead: the join key is the whole product.
  • Don't store every rendered prompt by default.
    ↳ Why it's tempting: it's the tracer's default, and you may need that text during an incident.
    ↳ What goes wrong: you've built a store of personal data with retention and access duties you never planned.
    ↳ Do instead: sample, redact, set a short lifetime, and keep failures at a higher rate than successes.
  • Don't build a bespoke schema or a streaming platform for one feature.
    ↳ Why it's tempting: your fields feel specific, and the convention is still marked Development.
    ↳ What goes wrong: your traces fit no tool, or you run a data pipeline for a prompt that a log line could serve.
    ↳ Do instead: the simpler rung: structured logs with the standard names, then your own under your namespace.
  • Not the same: prompt observability vs platform observability
    ↳ Why they get mixed up: both show up as traces in the same tool.
    ↳ Difference: the platform asks whether a request was slow or failed. The prompt view asks which version changed an outcome that returned 200.
    ↳ Think instead: same pipeline, with the prompt fields added.
  • Shelf life: two streams and the join key are durable. Attribute names may change, since the conventions moved repositories in 2026 and are still marked Development.

Connections

Path:prompt versioningdecoupled releaseprompt observabilityprompt governance
  • Owned elsewhere: LLM observability (LLM-Production) owns tracing and dashboards; agent tracing owns agent runs.
  • Builds on prompt versioning: the version id is the join key.
  • Used by A/B testing: per-version outcomes are its raw data.
  • Costed in cost modelling: tokens per version feed the sum.
  • Enforced by PII handling: redaction before the text store.
  • Drilled in a prompt that failed in production.

notes.title: Prompt Governance — Anyone May Draft, Few May Promote, Every Move Leaves a Record
notes.html:
References

Langfuse: prompt version control · GitHub: about code owners

TL;DR

Separate two rights: writing a version and promoting one. Promotion is a privileged, logged act. Otherwise the eval gate is only advice, and an incident starts with archaeology.

Stage:decidewriteassemblecallshapeevaluateshipwatchevery change

Recall

Prompt Answer
The two rights to separate? Authoring a version and promoting one.
Governance in a code-first setup? CODEOWNERS plus required review on the prompts directory.
What must an audit entry hold? Who, what, when, and the state before and after.

The idea

At 3 am a metric falls, and someone asks who moved production, to what, and why. Without a record, the incident stalls. Let anyone with domain knowledge draft, and let few promote. A registry calls this a protected label; a repo gets it from code owners and a required review. Both are enforced outside the model. Keeping decisions reproducible for a regulator is compliance and auditability.

Evolution

2010s code owners and protected branches ─▶ by 2026 protected labels and audit logs in registries. 🟢 Established (Oct 2026): separation of duties applied to text. In Langfuse both are paid tiers (chapter map, Landscape).

Code

# CODEOWNERS: a pull request touching prompts needs this team's approval
/prompts/   @acme/prompt-owners
/golden/    @acme/prompt-owners
